extracted.intended_audience: fans, media researchers, and TV programmers interested in Adult Swim's programming and promotional practices
extracted.subtask_description: Describes Adult Swim's programming strategies, stunts (especially April Fools' events), interactive campaigns, streaming/VOD policies, and block curation practices used to select and present content. Useful for understanding how the network stages pranks, ARGs, live streams, and international/local distribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: April Fools' Day prank format
rubrics_metrics.description: Annual tradition since 2004 of tricking the audience by altering programs or airing different/obscure programming beginning at 12 a.m. ET (technically March 31 schedule) with occasional additional pranks on April 1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pranks are often simulcast (Canada since 2019) and streamed to Adult Swim's YouTube (since 2021). Examples: drawing random mustaches on characters then re-airing clean versions; airing unfinished pilots instead of scheduled shows; swapping entire lineups; repeating or looping unexpected premieres; using network branding changes (e.g., '[meow meow]' logo). The description includes chronology of examples (2004–2026) demonstrating a wide range of tactics and escalations.

rubrics_metrics.name: April Fools' stunt tactics and presentation techniques
rubrics_metrics.description: Techniques used during pranks to create disorientation, surprise, or humor in programming presentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include adding absurd audio (fart noises, laugh tracks, pitch-shifted filters), editing to appear degraded (bad fansubs, reversed/chronological manipulation), picture-in-picture minimization, censor boxes on sex scenes, changing parental ratings, reanimating or re-dubbing content, superimposing game elements (coins/points), swapping hosts between streams, and altering logos or on-screen text. Use of bumps, promos, and outtakes between programs is frequent to tease or extend the gag.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of special premieres/stealth premieres and sneak peeks
rubrics_metrics.description: Replacing scheduled programming with early/unannounced showings of pilots, rough cuts, sneak peeks, or stealth premieres to generate buzz or misdirect viewers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: airing early rough cuts (Squidbillies pilot), showing only two minutes of a movie then minimizing it, or running unfinished sneak peeks and pilots in lieu of expected content. Often accompanied by announcements or later airing of the promised content to preserve viewer goodwill.

rubrics_metrics.name: ARG (Alternate Reality Game) campaign structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Design and rollout characteristics of Adult Swim's ARG campaigns used as network promotions and interactive narratives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical structure: broadcast a cryptic bump/transmission during a program, refer viewers to social accounts, provide puzzles weekly via bumps, accept solutions via Twitter (or other social), confirm solutions through subsequent bumps/accounts, and advance narrative chapters (e.g., Delilah/Amelia/Tristan story). Campaigns may rebrand accounts as part of narrative, introduce multiple social accounts, and run on a consistent cadence (weekly transmissions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Programming block curation principles (general)
rubrics_metrics.description: How Adult Swim organizes and curates programming blocks (originals, syndicated, anime, throwback blocks).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Blocks combine original shows, syndicated animated sitcoms, and acquired anime. Curation choices reflect target audiences (late-night adults, nostalgia viewers) and can shift over time (e.g., moving anime into Toonami). Examples: maintaining a mix of parody/remake heritage titles and later hits (Rick and Morty, Robot Chicken). Blocks may be relaunched, shortened, or discontinued based on strategy and rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Toonami block characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: Design and operational traits for Toonami as a 'block-within-a-block' specializing in anime and action programming.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typically airs Saturday nights, is hosted by TOM and SARA, stages 'Total Immersion Events' that change setting/hosts, and can include subpolicy exceptions (e.g., airing anime in Japanese with English subtitles despite prior dub-only norms). Toonami may feature game reviews, promos, and themed bumpers; its schedule changes can be used as major programming stunts or to revive interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nostalgia/throwback block curation (Checkered Past)
rubrics_metrics.description: Criteria for a nostalgia-focused animation block that airs older Cartoon Network original series from the 1990s and 2000s.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Format and running time are specified (initially 2 hours, later 1 hour). Naming and branding reference legacy motifs (checkerboard). Program selection prioritizes Cartoon Network originals ('Cartoon Cartoons') and aims for nostalgia appeal; scheduling and runtime can be adjusted or temporarily discontinued and later returned.

rubrics_metrics.name: Video on demand and streaming release policy
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules and timing for online VOD availability and evolution of access requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historically: online episodes appeared 1–3 days after broadcast (later a week), introduction of TV Everywhere authentication in August 2011 reduced free content, VOD combined into mobile app in 2014. Platform rights shift over time (Hulu, HBO Max/Max, etc.), causing some episodes to be removed or moved between services. Guidance highlights that licensing and platform agreements determine what is available and when.

rubrics_metrics.name: Live streams and interactive web series features
rubrics_metrics.description: Design elements for Adult Swim's online live stream offerings and web originals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common features: 24/7 marathons, chatrooms (similar to Twitch), live calls from viewers, real-time scoring/games, host interactivity, and occasional live Q&As with creators. Examples: FishCenter Live (points scored via fish interactions), shows accepting caller changes to program course, and marathons looped with edited versions broadcast later ('Williams Stream'). Many web series were cancelled by November 2020, but interactive formats influenced later programming and spinoffs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characteristics of Adult Swim Streams original shows
rubrics_metrics.description: Stylistic and format tendencies of online-exclusive original programs produced for the streams.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Often parody formats (e.g., FishCenter Live as a SportsCenter parody), mixture of surreal/disturbing content, experiments with format (crossword-solving show Bloodfeast with animations and poetry), and use of special effects. Many accepted viewer participation; some spawned TV spinoffs (Tender Touches, Gēmusetto).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mobile and OTT application availability and authentication
rubrics_metrics.description: Platform support and access control for Adult Swim apps and OTT distribution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apps available on Amazon Fire TV, Android (including Android TV), Apple TV, iOS, Chromecast, Roku, Xbox One; access to live simulcast and many episodes requires subscription-TV provider or OTT-platform credentials due to licensing. Geographic availability and content access are limited by licensing agreements.

rubrics_metrics.name: International distribution and localization constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Guidelines for international launches, local partnerships, and content restrictions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adult Swim localizes by licensing to local broadcasters or launching localized channels/blocks depending on market and legal/regulatory conditions (e.g., Ofcom in the UK). Programming may be absent from Cartoon Network in some markets and instead appear on other channels or streaming platforms; availability varies by country and over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Live events and festival programming principles
rubrics_metrics.description: How Adult Swim stages live events and festivals to extend brand presence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Events mix music, comedy, panels, and performances; have appeared at Comic-Con and as standalone festivals. Format adapts to circumstances (in-person in LA/Philadelphia, virtual during COVID-19). Selected performances may be streamed; events can be scaled or omitted year-to-year.

rubrics_metrics.name: Music partnerships and use in branding
rubrics_metrics.description: Adult Swim's collaboration approach with independent music labels and use of music in bumps and packaging.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Partnerships/co-produced compilations with labels (Stones Throw, Ghostly International, etc.) and use of instrumental/electronic music in bumps. Music is often licensed from a range of labels (Warp, Ninja Tune) and contributes to network identity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Game publishing and IP/licensing handling
rubrics_metrics.description: Adult Swim Games' focus and the later handling of title rights and storefront presence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Originally published Flash/web games and mobile titles; later formed a games division (2011) focused on indie/hardcore gamer market. Post-2020: relinquished rights to many games back to developers, delisted titles when rights/contact lost, and shut down the games website in 2026. IP management and developer relations determine long-term availability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Website features, user accounts, and commerce
rubrics_metrics.description: Elements that the Adult Swim official website historically provided to engage fans and monetize content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Features included full episodes, streams, podcasts, music, comics, a schedule, Toonami section, user accounts (messaging boards, profiles, live stream chat), and an online shop (Adult Swim Shop, As Seen on Adult Swim). User accounts and chat features were phased out (accounts disabled Jan 2021), and the site/store operations changed over time in response to strategy and platform shifts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Podcasting and supplementary audio/video content
rubrics_metrics.description: Approach to producing podcasts and behind-the-scenes content tied to the network.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: video podcast on iTunes (2006) with behind-the-scenes features; Adult Swim Podcast (2019) interviewing contributors; some podcasts and collaborations (This is Branchburg season 2) produced with partners. Releases can be intermittent and links/content may later be removed.
